sections.title: Device and OS Vulnerabilities
sections.content:
OPERATING SYSTEM VULNERABILITY OVERVIEW
OS | Common Vulnerability Sources
Windows | Buffer overflows, input validation problems, privilege flaws; largest install base = biggest target
macOS | UNIX-based architecture; weaknesses in access controls, secure boot, third-party software; perceived "safer" → complacency risk
Linux | Kernel vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, unpatched systems; rapid open-source patching, but widespread cloud/server use raises stakes
Android | Open source like Linux; fragmented across manufacturers/versions → inconsistent patching
iOS | Not open source, but still hit by significant vulnerabilities
NOTABLE EXAMPLE OS VULNERABILITIES
Vulnerability | OS | Description
MS08-067 | Windows | Windows Server Service RCE flaw; exploited by the Conficker worm (2008)
MS17-010 / EternalBlue | Windows | SMB protocol flaw enabling RCE; used in the WannaCry ransomware attack (May 2017)
Shellshock | macOS (Unix-based) | 2014 Bash shell flaw allowing system control
Stagefright | Android | 2015 flaw executing code via crafted MMS message (media library)
Project Zero iOS exploits | iOS | 2019 "watering hole" attacks via malicious websites, used by nation-states
Heartbleed | Linux (OpenSSL) | 2014 flaw allowing attackers to read system memory, exposing secret keys
LEGACY AND END-OF-LIFE (EOL) SYSTEMS
Term | Definition
EOL System | Product/version publicly declared no longer supported by vendor; no more updates/patches
Legacy System | Outdated tech still in use; not necessarily unsupported, but incompatible with newer architectures
• EOL and legacy overlap but aren't identical — an EOL system may still be a legacy system, and vice versa
• Example: Windows 7 / Server 2008 — stopped receiving updates January 2020, still widely used
• Secondhand/recertified/renewed devices often carry known unremediated firmware/driver flaws
• Replacement decisions must weigh: vendor support, warranty, marketplace reputation, transition/licensing/hardware costs, compatibility, data migration
FIRMWARE AND VIRTUALIZATION VULNERABILITIES
Vulnerability | Description
Meltdown / Spectre (2018) | Processor-level flaws allowing malicious programs to steal data mid-processing
LoJax (2018) | UEFI firmware flaw allowing persistence even after HDD replacement/OS reinstall
VM Escape | Attacker breaks out of a VM's isolated environment into the host or other VMs
Cloudburst (CVE-2009-1244) | VMware ESX Server flaw in VM display function allowing guest OS to execute code on host
Resource Reuse | Sensitive data leaks between VMs when disk/memory isn't sanitized between deployments
Hypervisor risk: management interfaces are attack vectors if insecure (weak auth, no encryption, protocol flaws). Mitigations for resource reuse: data sanitization, encryption throughout lifecycle, key management, resource segregation by security level.
ZERO-DAY VULNERABILITIES
Previously unknown flaws exploitable before vendors are aware/can patch. Traditional signature-based tools (AV, firewalls) are often ineffective against them.
• Favored by advanced threat actors (organized crime, nation-states) for high-value targeted attacks
• Responsible disclosure — researchers privately inform vendor before public disclosure
• High financial value (a mobile OS zero-day can be worth millions); state agencies stockpile them
MISCONFIGURATION VULNERABILITIES
Common causes: unnecessary services enabled, default/guessable credentials, overly permissive settings, publicly-accessible cloud storage/compute by default.
• Support/troubleshooting activity can inadvertently leave security features disabled or access controls loosened
• Urgent outage response often bypasses change management (no documentation/testing/approval) → misconfiguration risk
CRYPTOGRAPHIC VULNERABILITIES
Example | Issue
MD5 / SHA-1 | Now insecure — vulnerable to collision attacks
Heartbleed | OpenSSL library flaw allowing attackers to read secure communications
KRACK | Key Reinstallation Attack against WPA2, intercepts/decrypts Wi-Fi traffic
DES | 56-bit key, vulnerable to brute force; replaced by 3DES then AES
Sweet32 (CVE-2016-2183) | Birthday attack against 3DES (2016); NIST deprecated 3DES in 2017
BEAST / POODLE | Attacks exploiting SSL/early TLS cipher suite implementation flaws
• RSA vulnerable if small key sizes or weak random number generation used; reused key pairs increase compromise risk over time
• Kerckhoffs's principle — a cryptosystem should stay secure even if everything except the key is public knowledge
• Key protection practices: HSMs, key management systems (KMS), access controls/authentication, monitoring/auditing key usage, periodic key rotation
MOBILE DEVICE VULNERABILITIES: ROOTING, JAILBREAKING, SIDELOADING
Term | Platform | Description
Rooting | Android | Gaining root/admin access to modify system files, install custom ROMs
Jailbreaking | iOS | Removing Apple's restrictions to install unauthorized apps, access system files
Sideloading | Mostly Android (APK files) | Installing apps outside the official app store; on Apple devices, voids warranty and violates ToS
• Sideloaded/unofficial apps skip official vetting — higher malware/data theft/privacy risk
• Excessive app permissions increase attack surface beyond the app's legitimate purpose
• Regulated industries (healthcare, finance) should strictly prohibit rooting/jailbreaking/sideloading
• MDM platforms can detect and restrict these behaviors; combine with employee awareness training

sections.title: Application and Cloud Vulnerabilities
sections.content:
RACE CONDITIONS AND TOCTOU
Race condition — software flaw where operations that must execute in a specific order can be manipulated, causing unpredictable outcomes.
• TOCTOU (Time-Of-Check to Time-Of-Use) — system state changes between the check (verification) and use (execution) steps
• Mitigated via atomic operations (check + execute as a single indivisible step), locks, semaphores, monitors
Example CVE | Description
Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195) | Linux kernel race condition allowing local privilege escalation
CVE-2020-0796 | Windows SMBv3 (SMBGhost) race condition allowing arbitrary code execution
MEMORY INJECTION AND BUFFER OVERFLOW
Memory injection — attacker introduces malicious code into a running process's memory, running with that process's privilege level. Common forms: buffer overflow, format string vulnerabilities, code injection.
Buffer overflow — attacker overfills a reserved memory buffer; a stack overflow can overwrite the return address to redirect execution to attacker code.
• Mitigations: ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization), DEP (Data Execution Prevention), type-safe languages, secure coding practices
MALICIOUS UPDATES
Update that appears legitimate but carries harmful code — exploits user trust in the update process.
Example | Description
CCleaner (2017) | Legitimate software compromised with an unauthorized malicious update
SolarWinds (2020) | Orion platform update distributed a backdoor to government/corporate networks
Mitigations: secure software supply chain management, digital signature verification.
EVALUATION SCOPE / TARGET OF EVALUATION (TOE)
TOE Practice | Description
Security Testing | Vulnerability assessments and pen testing
Documentation Review | Design specs, architecture diagrams, security policies
Source Code Analysis | Identifies vulnerabilities/coding errors, input validation issues
Configuration Assessment | Access controls, encryption settings, authentication mechanisms
Cryptographic Analysis | Encryption algorithms, key management, secure key storage
Compliance Verification | Verifies adherence to regulations/frameworks/certifications
Security Architecture Review | Identifies gaps like insufficient segregation of duties, missing audit trails
• For a penetration tester, scope = authorized boundaries for testing
• For an attacker, scope = the intended target
WEB APPLICATION ATTACKS
HTTP is stateless — apps must manage sessions via cookies/session IDs. Improper session management (predictable IDs, session fixation/hijacking) enables CSRF and XSS.
Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) types:
Type | Mechanism
Reflected/Nonpersistent | Malicious script delivered via a crafted URL/link; executes once when clicked
Stored/Persistent | Malicious script inserted into a back-end database/CMS; executes for every viewer
DOM-based | Exploits client-side scripts manipulating the Document Object Model directly
SQL Injection (SQLi) — attacker modifies SQL statements (SELECT/INSERT/DELETE/UPDATE) via unsanitized input to extract/insert data or execute code with the database app's privileges.
• Classic example: entering ' or 1=1# into a username field turns a query into an always-true statement, dumping all records
CLOUD-BASED APPLICATION ATTACKS
• Shared responsibility model confusion can leave security gaps
• Side-channel attacks — attacker on the same physical server as the victim extracts info via shared resources
• Misconfigured storage buckets → unauthorized data access
• Cryptojacking — using cloud processing power to mine cryptocurrency without consent, driving up costs/degrading performance
• Cloud can also be used as an attack platform — fraudulent sites, malicious file hosting for phishing distribution
CLOUD ACCESS SECURITY BROKER (CASB)
Enterprise software mediating access to cloud services across devices.
CASB functions: SSO/access control enforcement, malware/rogue device scanning, user/resource activity monitoring, data exfiltration mitigation.
CASB Deployment Mode | Description
Forward Proxy | At client network edge; inspects traffic in real time; risk of bypass, potential bottleneck
Reverse Proxy | At cloud network edge; no client device config needed; requires cloud app proxy support
API-based | Brokers connections via cloud service API (e.g., propagates account disablement to the cloud); depends on API feature support
SOFTWARE SUPPLY CHAIN
Supply Chain Component | Risk
Service Providers | Cloud services/dev agencies — risk from inadequate security or insecure communications
Hardware Suppliers | Preinstalled vulnerable firmware, physical tampering, unreliable/outdated drivers
Software Providers | Vulnerable or outdated third-party libraries/frameworks/components
Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) — comprehensive inventory of all components in a software product (names, versions, suppliers). Enables:
• Identifying vulnerable third-party components before exploitation
• Verifying component origin/trust
• Rapid response after a vulnerability disclosure
SBOM/dependency tools:
Tool/Standard | Purpose
OWASP Dependency-Check | Software Composition Analysis (SCA) — identifies dependencies and known vulnerabilities
OWASP Dependency-Track | Consumes Dependency-Check output for fuller SBOM management
SPDX | Open standard for SBOM data (component ID, licensing, security references)
CycloneDX | Lightweight SBOM specification

sections.title: Vulnerability Identification Methods
sections.content:
VULNERABILITY SCANNING BASICS
Systematic probing of systems/networks with specialized tools, run internally and externally, to detect known vulnerabilities (missing patches, misconfigurations, outdated software).
Tool | Focus
Nessus / OpenVAS | Network vulnerability scanning — hosts, mobile devices, servers, routers, switches
Application scanners | Static analysis (code, not executing) and dynamic analysis (running app) — finds unvalidated input, broken access controls, SQLi
CREDENTIALED VS. NON-CREDENTIALED SCANS
Scan Type | Access Level | Use Case
Non-Credentialed | No OS/app login; sees what an unprivileged network user sees | External perimeter assessment, web app scanning
Credentialed | Login rights + relevant permissions | Deeper analysis, detects misconfigurations, simulates insider/compromised-account attack; more intrusive
PACKAGE MONITORING
Tracks security of third-party packages/libraries/dependencies, tied to SBOM and software supply chain risk management. SCA tools compare inventory against vulnerability databases (e.g., NVD) continuously; often paired with governance policies (audits, approval processes for new packages).
THREAT FEEDS AND INTELLIGENCE
Concept | Description
Threat Feed | Real-time, continuously updated info on threats/vulnerabilities from multiple sources
Open-Source Feeds | Cyber Threat Alliance, MISP — free, less depth than proprietary
Proprietary Feeds | IBM X-Force Exchange, Mandiant FireEye, Recorded Future — deeper analysis, paid
Information-Sharing Orgs | Cyber Threat Alliance, ISACs (industry-specific) — collaborative threat data exchange
Threat intelligence output forms:
• Behavioral Threat Research — narrative commentary on attacks/TTPs
• Reputational Threat Intelligence — malicious IP/domain lists, malware signatures
• Threat Data — machine-correlatable data matching customer logs to known TTPs/indicators
OSINT (Open-Source Intelligence) — collecting/analyzing publicly available info for decision-making.
OSINT Tool | Purpose
Shodan | Investigating Internet-connected devices
Maltego | Visualizing complex information networks
Recon-ng | Web-based reconnaissance
theHarvester | Gathering emails/subdomains/hosts/employee names
DEEP WEB AND DARK WEB
Term | Definition
Deep Web | Any part of the web not indexed by search engines (registration-gated, unlinked, nonstandard DNS)
Dark Net | Anonymizing overlay network (Tor, Freenet, I2P) hiding network existence/activity
Dark Web | Sites/content/services accessible only via a dark net
Legitimate dark web uses: privacy/anonymity for whistleblowers/journalists/activists, bypassing censorship, research into criminal TTPs.
PENETRATION TESTING
Test Environment Knowledge | Formerly Called | Description
Unknown Environment | Black Box | No privileged info; extensive recon needed; simulates external threat
Known Environment | White Box | Complete network access/info; simulates privileged insider threat
Partially Known Environment | Gray Box | Some info; partial recon needed
• Penetration testing excels at chained vulnerabilities, authentication bypass, and design/logic flaws automated scanners miss
• Bug bounty programs — crowdsourced testing via rewards to external researchers; broader/more diverse coverage than a hired pen test team, but less predictable in cost/timeline
• Responsible disclosure programs — guidelines/procedures + rewards for reporting vulnerabilities before malicious exploitation
AUDITING
• Product audits — focus on specific features (e.g., application code)
• System/process audits — wider scope (supply chain, config, support, monitoring, cybersecurity)
Audit Type | Focus
Compliance Audit | Adherence to regulations (GDPR, HIPAA)
Risk-Based Audit | Potential threats/vulnerabilities in systems/processes
Technical Audit | IT infrastructure specifics — network security, access controls, data protection
Penetration testing is a critical component of technical audits; some regulations (e.g., PCI DSS) mandate annual/proactive pen testing.

sections.title: Vulnerability Analysis and Remediation
sections.content:
CVE, CVSS, AND THE NVD
System | Role
CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) | Dictionary of known vulnerabilities; format CVE-YYYY-#### + description, references, creation date
NVD (National Vulnerability Database) | NIST repository built on CVE; adds analysis, criticality metric, fix info
CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) | Maintained by FIRST; scores 0–10 based on exploitability/impact factors
SCAP (Security Content Automation Protocol) | Delivers vulnerability feed updates; compares config against secure baseline
CVSS Score Bands:
Score | Description
0.1+ | Low
4.0+ | Medium
7.0+ | High
9.0+ | Critical
• Nessus calls its feeds "plug-ins"; OpenVAS calls them "network vulnerability tests (NVTs)"
FALSE POSITIVES, FALSE NEGATIVES, AND VALIDATION
Term | Meaning
False Positive | Scanner incorrectly flags something as a vulnerability
False Negative | An actual vulnerability goes undetected
• Excessive false positives risk causing scans to be disregarded entirely
• Mitigate false negatives via repeat scans and multiple scanner vendors
• Log review helps validate whether a flagged vulnerability is genuine (e.g., matching event log crash entries to a scanner-flagged unstable process)
VULNERABILITY ANALYSIS FACTORS
Factor | Description
Prioritization | Based on severity, ease of exploitation, potential impact
Classification | Categorize by affected system/app type, nature, potential impact
Exposure Factor (EF) | Extent an asset is susceptible to a specific vulnerability being exploited
Impacts | Financial loss, reputational damage, operational disruption, regulatory penalties
Environmental Variables | IT infrastructure diversity/age, external threat landscape, regulatory environment, operational practices
Risk Tolerance | Org's acceptable risk level — must align vulnerability response with overall risk strategy
REMEDIATION PRACTICES
Practice | Description
Patching | Applying updates/patches to fix known vulnerabilities; needs centralized patch management
Cybersecurity Insurance | Doesn't fix vulnerabilities, but provides financial protection/risk transfer for breaches
Segmentation | Divides network into segments to contain breaches, limits lateral movement
Compensating Controls | Alternative mitigations when direct remediation isn't possible (extra monitoring, secondary auth, enhanced encryption)
Exceptions/Exemptions | Risk accepted by leadership when remediation isn't feasible (business/technical/cost constraints); documented with reassessment timeline
VALIDATION METHODS
Method | Purpose
Re-scanning | Additional scan post-remediation to confirm the vulnerability is gone
Audit | In-depth review of remediation steps against policy/best practices, confirms documentation updated
Verification | Confirms remediation results via manual checks, automated testing, or log review
VULNERABILITY REPORTING
Comprehensive reports rank vulnerabilities by severity/impact (using CVSS for standardized comparison), describe possible exploitation outcomes, and recommend specific remediation actions. Timely, clear reporting (for both technical and nontechnical stakeholders) reduces the attacker's window of opportunity.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.content:
• Identify procedures/tools required to scan for vulnerabilities — passive network scanners, active remote/agent-based scanners, application/web application scanners
• Develop a configuration and maintenance plan to keep vulnerability and threat feeds updated
• Run scans regularly; review results for false positives/negatives, using log review and CVE data to validate findings
• Schedule configuration reviews and remediation plans, using CVSS criticality to prioritize actions
• Implement threat analysis platforms; monitor advisories and bulletins for new threat sources
• Implement penetration testing exercises with a clearly defined project scope

concept_cards.hook: Vulnerability scan using credentials for a deeper audit.
Publicly available info plus tools to aggregate/search it.

practice_questions.q: A web form lets users enter text that ends up in a database query, and an attacker enters ' OR 1=1 --. What vulnerability is this?
practice_questions.explanation: Unsanitized input inserted into SQL queries allows injection.

practice_questions.q: A tool scans servers and reports missing patches and known vulnerabilities. What is it?
A comment field lets an attacker store JavaScript that runs in other users' browsers. What vulnerability is this?
practice_questions.explanation: XSS injects script that runs in victims' browsers.

practice_questions.q: A scan uses administrator credentials to log in and check installed software in detail. What scan type is this?
practice_questions.explanation: Credentialed scans see more than external scans.

practice_questions.q: A program writes more data into a memory buffer than it can hold, overwriting nearby memory. What is this?
practice_questions.explanation: Overflowing a buffer can let an attacker overwrite memory and run code.

practice_questions.q: A scanner reports a vulnerability that does not actually exist on the system. What is this?
practice_questions.explanation: A false positive is an alert for something that is not there.

practice_questions.q: A program checks a file's permissions, then opens it a moment later; an attacker swaps the file in between. What vulnerability is this?
practice_questions.explanation: TOCTOU exploits the gap between checking and using a resource.

practice_questions.q: A real vulnerability exists, but the scanner fails to report it. What is this?
practice_questions.explanation: False negatives are missed real issues.

practice_questions.q: A vulnerability is being exploited before the vendor knows about it or has a patch. What is it called?
practice_questions.explanation: Zero-days have no available fix when exploited.

practice_questions.q: Which scoring system rates vulnerability severity from 0 to 10?
practice_questions.explanation: CVSS scores severity; CVE identifies the vulnerability.
